First listed 2025-06-20 · episode or wrap

Earnings, Geopolitics, and Sectors - The Friday Market Wrap!

The June 20 wrap is cautious on solar and homebuilders, while distinguishing weak housing demand from a mortgage credit crisis. Eisman again declines to call private credit a bubble, but overstates how little credit-quality information exists. His core tool is to separate the growth of lending from the quality of the loans.

YouTube · 2025-06-20 ↗Substack · 2025-06-21 ↗
The housing affordability and incentive diagnosis has strong support. The solar view is conditional on policy and should not be treated as a fixed 2029 short. His mortgage-payment arithmetic and blanket private-credit data assertion need correction.

youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c006 · explanation

Current housing weakness is primarily affordability and mortgage-rate lock-in, not a repeat of subprime credit deterioration.

Right
Source · 7:08-7:58 ↗
SpeakerSteve Eisman
Stanceasserted
Horizonnot stated
Materialitymajor

FHFA research supports lock-in and OCC servicing data show a high current-loan share. These support the distinction, while not guaranteeing every borrower is sound.

Assessment test: Track affordability, listings, delinquencies and underwriting separately.

Evidence and assessment details

Attribution confidence: high. Assessment confidence: medium. Thesis family: housing.

  • The Lock-In Effect of Rising Mortgage Rates, Working Paper 24-03 · 2024-03-18
    Primary loan-level research estimates higher market rates relative to existing loans reduce sale probability. Original abstract estimates 1.33 million prevented sales in 2022Q2-2023Q4 and upward price pressure from reduced supply. Estimates support the mechanism, not every December 2025 market statistic.
  • Mortgage performance in second-quarter 2025
    Within the covered servicer sample, 97.5% of loans were current and performing at quarter-end, versus 97.3% a year earlier. The sample does not cover every US mortgage.
youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c007 · explanation

Moving from a 3% mortgage to 7% requires roughly halving the home price to keep the same payment.

Wrong
Source · 7:37-7:48 ↗
SpeakerSteve Eisman
Stanceasserted
Horizonnot stated
Materialitysupporting

For a fixed 30-year amortizing principal-and-interest loan, the affordable principal falls about 36.6%, not 50%. Taxes, insurance and down payments change the full household calculation.

Conditional reasoning

Monthly payment factor is r/(1-(1+r)^-360). Factors at 3% and 7% are approximately 0.004216 and 0.006653, so new principal is 0.6337 of old principal.

  • 30-year fully amortizing fixed-rate loans
  • Same principal-and-interest payment; exclude taxes and insurance

Assessment test: Hold loan term and monthly principal-and-interest payment constant.

Evidence and assessment details

Attribution confidence: high. Assessment confidence: medium. Thesis family: mortgage_math.

No independent empirical outcome evidence is attached. A principle, disclosure or unfinished forecast is not a verified investment win.

Evidence and assessment details

Attribution confidence: high. Assessment confidence: medium. Thesis family: credit_cycles.

  • Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13 · 2011-01-27
    Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

How he reasons here

  • Separate housing demand from mortgage default risk.
  • Trace subsidies and financing rates through customer affordability.
  • Follow loan quality as well as loan growth.
  • Do not equate opacity with demonstrated fraud or a proven bubble.
